questions.question: What do the conflict markers in a Git conflict look like and what do they mean?
questions.title: Understanding Git Conflict Markers
questions.direct_answer: Git marks conflicts with '<<<<<<<' (start of your changes), '=======' (separator), and '>>>>>>>' (end of incoming changes) — you resolve the conflict by editing the file to keep the desired version and removing the markers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Git experience — have you actually resolved a conflict or just read about it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Committing the file with conflict markers still in it — this compiles but breaks logic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that some markers include the common ancestor (with '|||||' section) when using diff3 conflict style

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When a merge conflict happens, Git modifies the conflicted file with special markers that look like this: seven less-than signs followed by HEAD — that's the start of your current branch's version. Then seven equal signs as a separator. Then the other version below it. Then seven greater-than signs followed by the branch name being merged in. Everything between the less-than signs and the equals signs is your version. Everything between the equals signs and the greater-than signs is the incoming version from the other branch. To resolve, you manually edit the file to contain what you actually want — which might be your version, their version, or a combination of both — and then delete all the marker lines. There should be no '<<<<<<<', '=======', or '>>>>>>>' left in the file when you're done. A common mistake is accidentally committing the markers — the code might compile but the logic will be wrong. After resolving, you run 'git add' on the resolved file and then 'git commit' to complete the merge.

sections.title: Key Points
content: '<<<<<<< HEAD': start of your current branch's conflicting section
'=======': separator between the two conflicting versions
'>>>>>>> branch-name': end of the incoming branch's conflicting section
Resolution: edit file to desired content, remove ALL markers, then git add + git commit
Never commit a file with conflict markers still in it — it will break your code

questions.question: What is the step-by-step process for resolving a Git merge conflict?
questions.title: How to Resolve a Git Merge Conflict
questions.direct_answer: Identify conflicted files with git status, open each file and edit to resolve the conflict markers, git add the resolved files, then git commit to finalize the merge.

interviewer_intent.testing: Hands-on Git experience — can the candidate walk through the resolution process confidently
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to 'git add' the resolved files before 'git commit' — the merge stays incomplete
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that 'git merge --abort' lets you cancel the merge entirely and return to the pre-merge state

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When a merge fails due to conflicts, here's the process. Step one: run 'git status' — it shows you a list of files with 'both modified' status, which are the conflicted ones. Step two: open each conflicted file and find the conflict markers. Read both versions carefully and decide what the file should look like — keep your version, keep their version, or write a combined version that incorporates both changes. Delete all the marker lines. Step three: once a file is resolved, run 'git add filename' to mark it as resolved in Git's staging area. Step four: after all conflicted files are resolved and staged, run 'git commit'. Git will pre-populate a merge commit message. Save it. If at any point during the process things are getting complicated or you're unsure what to keep, you can run 'git merge --abort' which completely cancels the merge and returns your repository to the state before you started the merge. This is your escape hatch.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Step 1: 'git status' — see which files show 'both modified'
Step 2: Edit conflicted files — remove markers, keep correct content
Step 3: 'git add filename' — mark each file as resolved
Step 4: 'git commit' — finalizes the merge with a merge commit
'git merge --abort': cancel the merge entirely and return to pre-merge state

questions.question: How can you prevent or minimize merge conflicts in a team setting?
questions.title: Preventing Merge Conflicts
questions.direct_answer: Minimize conflicts by keeping branches short-lived, pulling or fetching from main frequently to stay in sync, communicating with teammates about shared files, and following modular code design to reduce overlapping changes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Team awareness and proactive thinking — separates reactive coders from collaborative engineers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking conflicts are unavoidable and normal — they are, but many can be prevented with good habits
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that architectural decisions like microservices or modular code ownership reduce the surface area for conflicts

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Conflicts are somewhat inevitable in team development, but you can minimize them significantly with good habits. First, keep feature branches short-lived — the longer a branch lives, the more it drifts from main and the worse the conflict will be when you finally merge. Aim to merge within days, not weeks. Second, pull from main (or rebase onto main) frequently — at least daily on active branches. This surfaces small conflicts early when they're easy to resolve, rather than one giant conflict at the end. Third, communicate with your team — if you're about to make sweeping changes to a shared file, give people a heads-up so they can merge their current work first. Fourth, modular code design helps a lot — if every team member owns clearly separate modules and avoids touching the same files, conflicts simply can't happen. Finally, small focused PRs merge faster and have less surface area for conflict than big PRs that touch many files.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Keep branches short-lived — merge frequently, don't let branches drift for weeks
Pull or rebase from main regularly — surface conflicts early while they're small
Communicate: tell teammates before making changes to widely-shared files
Modular design reduces conflict surface area — clear file/module ownership per team member
Small, focused PRs merge faster and conflict less than large sweeping PRs

questions.question: What is git mergetool and how do IDE tools help with conflict resolution?
questions.title: Using git mergetool and IDEs for Conflict Resolution
questions.direct_answer: git mergetool launches a configured visual merge tool to resolve conflicts through a UI showing three panes (yours, base, theirs); modern IDEs like IntelliJ IDEA have built-in merge editors that do the same more conveniently.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical tooling awareness — do you know what's available beyond just text editing?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Resolving conflicts by randomly deleting lines without understanding what both branches were trying to do
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention VS Code's built-in conflict resolution UI and IntelliJ's three-pane merge editor as specific tools

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: While you can resolve conflicts by manually editing files with a text editor, visual tools make it significantly easier — especially for complex conflicts. 'git mergetool' is the Git command that launches your configured visual merge tool. You can configure it to use tools like vimdiff, kdiff3, meld, or anything else. But honestly, for most developers in 2024, the IDE is the best place to resolve conflicts. IntelliJ IDEA has an excellent three-pane merge editor: left pane shows your version, right pane shows the incoming version, center pane shows the base (common ancestor), and you get buttons to accept left, accept right, or accept both for each change. VS Code has a similar built-in conflict resolution UI with 'Accept Current Change', 'Accept Incoming Change', 'Accept Both Changes' buttons inline in the editor. These tools prevent the common mistake of accidentally deleting code you meant to keep — you can see both versions side by side and make deliberate decisions about each conflicting section.

sections.title: Key Points
content: 'git mergetool': launches configured visual merge tool from the terminal
IntelliJ IDEA: three-pane merge editor (local / base / remote) with accept buttons per conflict
VS Code: inline 'Accept Current/Incoming/Both' buttons in the editor
Visual tools prevent accidentally deleting code by showing both versions side by side
Configure your preferred tool: 'git config --global merge.tool vimdiff' (or another tool)

questions.question: How do rebase conflicts differ from merge conflicts?
questions.title: Rebase Conflicts vs Merge Conflicts
questions.direct_answer: Both show the same conflict markers, but during a rebase you may encounter conflicts on each commit being replayed (one at a time), while a merge surfaces all conflicts at once — and rebase conflicts are resolved with 'git rebase --continue' instead of 'git commit'.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of conflict resolution experience and understanding of the difference in workflow
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running 'git commit' after resolving a rebase conflict instead of 'git rebase --continue'
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that 'git rebase --skip' lets you skip a commit that is entirely superseded by the base branch

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The conflict markers look identical between merge and rebase conflicts — it's the resolution workflow that differs. During a merge, Git tries to combine everything at once and stops with all conflicts showing simultaneously. You resolve them all, do 'git add', and then 'git commit' to complete the merge. During a rebase, Git replays your commits one by one onto the new base. If a conflict occurs, it pauses on that specific commit. You resolve the conflict and stage the fixed files, but instead of 'git commit', you run 'git rebase --continue'. Then Git moves to the next commit and may pause again with another conflict. This continues until all commits have been replayed. It's more tedious if you have many conflicting commits. You have two escape hatches: 'git rebase --abort' goes back to where you started (before the rebase), and 'git rebase --skip' skips the current conflicting commit entirely (useful if the conflict is because a change on the base branch already incorporated what this commit was doing).

sections.title: Key Points
content: Merge conflicts: all at once, resolve all → git add → git commit
Rebase conflicts: one commit at a time, resolve → git add → git rebase --continue
NEVER run 'git commit' during a rebase conflict — use 'git rebase --continue'
'git rebase --abort': cancel the rebase and return to original state
'git rebase --skip': skip the current conflicting commit
